The gate of the Jing'an post office opened, as a rule, on the stroke of the Jing'an Temple bell. The postmen in their yellow khaki uniforms pedaled out in a swarm and soon scattered, like a flock of pigeons let loose.

Zhongliang was among them. His bicycle had been bought with that tuition money. It was the rule at the office: to be a postman you first had to furnish your own bicycle, both because it was no small piece of property and because the office would not spend more than it had to on any one carrier.

Zhongliang hung the two yellow canvas mailbags on the back of his bicycle. His work each day was to carry the letters inside them to where they were meant to go, and to bring back the letters from the pillar-boxes along the way and hand them in at the sorting-room window. From there the letters would fly like snowflakes to every part of the country and out to every corner of the world.

On his first day the postmaster told him, as he told everyone, that it was ordinary work: as long as a man had his hands and feet, as long as he could read and knew the roads, anyone could be a postman; and yet it was a remarkable work too, for it reached into every household. "A letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold," the postmaster said. "Sometimes a single letter is a whole sky."

Zhongliang nodded, and felt all at once an unspeakable desolation rise in him, a sense that his whole life would go paired with this yellow uniform. But his fellows soon found that this young man was nothing like his dead father. He was too aloof, too proud; a man like that had no business here at all.

Every morning the men gathered at the sorting-room door to wait for the mail, and women were a subject not to be avoided. A postman met so many people in a day, came and went before so many doors, that there were always a few doors that would stand half open to them, and always some women who would half yield. What Zhongliang could not stand was the way they told it afterward, so vividly, so shamelessly, as though every woman under heaven were meat laid out on a postman's block. It sickened him, and at such times he would often drift into Zhou San's gatehouse and lean silently against the edge of his desk.
Zhou San had been watching him a long time. This day he smiled and said, "You're not like your old man."
"Why should I be like him?" said Zhongliang.
Zhou San smiled again, pulled open a drawer, took out a letter, and said, "Drop this off on your way."

Zhongliang took the letter and saw at a glance that whoever had written it had copied the models of Huang Tingjian; but there was no recipient's name on the envelope, only a single line of address: No. 203, Siming Apartments, Rue Ratard.

His father had had him do this sort of thing more than once while he lived. The envelopes never carried names, and sometimes not even an address; his father only told him where to take them. Zhongliang had asked once, "Why send me? You're the postman."
Xu Delin had said, very impatient, "Take it where I tell you. What's all this talk for?"
Now Zhongliang finally understood. He held the envelope out to Zhou San and said, "You're all in it together."
Zhou San, still smiling broadly, pointed toward the sorting-room door and said, "We're all in it together. We all scrape our rice from the same pot."
"I'll report you," said Zhongliang.

"Report me to whom? The postmaster?" Zhou San let the smile fade slowly from his face, dropped his eyes to the desk, and said, "If you won't do the favor, put the letter down." With that he picked up the tea mug on the desk, took a sip, and, as though nothing at all had passed, told of a dream he'd had the night before, a snake as thick as this. He gestured to show it, then dug out some money and said to Zhongliang, "See a snake and you'll strike it rich, it's a lucky sign. Bring me back a lottery ticket when you come."
It was outside No. 203, Siming Apartments, on Rue Ratard, that Zhongliang first saw Su Lina.

She had plainly just risen from a nap, her hair loose, in a sleeveless chiffon nightdress. The two of them said not a word across the threshold. Zhongliang handed up the letter; she took it, glanced at it, then raised her eyes to him and softly pushed the door to. But that languid, indifferent look on her face left a deep mark on him.

Su Lina did not open the letter, for she knew there was nothing inside but a sheet of blank paper. She only pressed her ear to the door, listened to the postman going down the stairs step by step, and then walked slowly out to the balcony.

The summer sun glared on the balcony, and on the French plane trees down both sides of the street below. But she did not see the postman's departing back; she only heard a run of bicycle bells sound out through the thick leaves.

Su Lina went back into the room deep in thought, sat down in the cane chair, took the cigarette case from the tea table, drew one out, lit it, and held the letter idly to the lighter's flame; then she watched it turn to ash in a ball of fire.

Two hours later Su Lina sat in a café, for all the world a modern girl idling away her time, sipping her coffee, leafing through a pictorial, now and then gazing listlessly out at the street. When she saw Mr. Pan appear in the crowd, she raised a hand to call the waiter, paid, and left.

Su Lina followed Mr. Pan at a distance and watched him go into an office building; then she turned down a side lane and went in by the building's back door. They met in the corridor and, like two strangers, went up the stairs one behind the other, all the way to the rooftop terrace. Mr. Pan said, "Tell me how things stand on your side."
Su Lina said, "Yu Hongjun has given him a clear hint: once Shanghai falls, he's to go to Nanjing as an aide on the mayor's staff."
Mr. Pan nodded and said, "Then go to Nanjing with him."
"And if he won't take me?"
"You're his wife. You'll find a way to make him."
Su Lina said no more. She turned to look at the far spire of the Customs House clock tower.
Mr. Pan said, "Remember your task."
Su Lina turned back and said, "Don't worry. I know what I have to do."
Mr. Pan let out a breath, took the cigarette case from his pocket, one for each of them, and they lit up and smoked.

It was near dusk when Su Lina got home. She opened the door to find her husband, Zhou Chukang, sitting under the electric fan, and a man in a white linen shirt with a folding fan in his hand bent over him, saying something in his ear. Seeing her come in, the man unhurriedly straightened, nodded, and said, "Mrs. Zhou."

Su Lina remembered the face from her wedding, one of Zhou Chukang's fellows from the party academy, it seemed. Only after the man had taken his leave did she ask, "Who was that? Sneaking about like that."
Zhou Chukang might not have heard. He turned to draw the curtains, switched on the lamp, and asked, "Where did you go this afternoon?"
"Had a coffee, saw a film." As she spoke Su Lina turned toward the kitchen, but Zhou Chukang caught her from behind.

Zhou Chukang was urgent, worked up, the way he had been their first time in the room at the East Asia Hotel, pressing her onto the bed and taking her at once, too impatient even to get their clothes off.

Su Lina lay sweating in his arms a while, then rose and stripped herself bare. Just as she was going to the bathroom, Zhou Chukang reached out and caught her, said nothing, only drew her gently into his arms and pressed the two sweat-damp bodies close together.
Zhou Chukang said suddenly, "I'm leaving." Su Lina did not move, but something turned over inside her. His hand slid along the line of her body, and he said, "Tonight."
Su Lina lifted her face and said, "Shanghai's still standing."

"That's just it, to keep it standing." Zhou Chukang stopped her mouth with his, kissed her as if at a parting for life and death, lingering and heartbreaking. Neither spoke; silently they came together once more on the bed, and then Zhou Chukang rolled to one side, let out a long breath, and said, "I leave tonight. For the headquarters of the 88th Division, as chief of the operations section."
"Why?" Su Lina asked, her eyes wide on him.

"I was an army lieutenant colonel to begin with." Zhou Chukang smiled and wiped the sweat from her face. "What I studied in Japan was infantry command. Now at last it can be put to use." Su Lina said nothing, reached over and switched off the bedside lamp, and nestled against him like a child, both hands gripping one of his arms, listening to him tell how he had gone to find Chen Sunong, the chief of staff of the 88th. "He's my senior from the academy," Zhou Chukang said. "I told him that if he wouldn't let me back to my unit, I'd throttle that Japanese consul at the negotiating table with my own two hands."
That said, Zhou Chukang pushed her two hands gently aside in the dark, got up, and went to the bathroom. Over the rush of water he called to Su Lina, "Get my uniform out of the wardrobe."

Su Lina lay in bed without moving or making a sound, and watched him come out naked, switch on the light, open the wardrobe, and put the uniform on piece by piece, then stand before the mirror studying his own military bearing. All at once Su Lina sprang from the bed and rushed to throw her arms around him. Zhou Chukang gave way to her embrace, buried his face in her hair, and after a long while said in her ear, "I hope this time it takes, and you'll be carrying our child."
Su Lina did not move or speak, only held him tight, so tight she could hardly draw breath.
